cells.tense: What you've made is whole enough to be felt, and you're letting yourself feel it while the pen is still in your hand.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've already finished and say out loud, once, that it's done. Then let the saying show you where the next push actually belongs. It hands back a finish line you can stand on.
cells.core:
On an ordinary good week you can look at something you made and find it whole, and you let yourself feel the whole thing instead of hunting for the loose thread. Nothing there needs your worry now, and the not-worrying isn't a slip; it's what finishing is for.

That doesn't mean you stop making. It means the next thing starts from being satisfied with the last one, not from being afraid it wasn't enough. Stay in touch with what the making actually left in you, and let that set the pace instead of pushing through the feeling. What this balance feeds next is steadier drive, where what you want and what you do are pointed the same way.
cells.sheetLine: You finish things and you feel them. The next starts from there.
cells.verb: Feeling a thing through until it's whole, and knowing it's whole.
cells.place: The place where a thing is finished and let go from, which is also where the next one starts.

cells.tense: You're already braced for how you'll have to defend something that isn't finished, maybe hasn't even been made yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing that's done and leave it alone for a week, no edits and no checking. Let the week itself hold it. It loosens a grip that's been tiring you, and shows what holds without your hand on it.
cells.core:
On an ordinary good week you send something off and you know it holds: you've given the details enough care that they hold on their own, and you spend the next days on what's growing rather than on what's already grown.

Running ahead of that, wanting to do well can tip into holding on too tight, where nothing you've finished is allowed to be finished yet, and you're bracing for the next push before the last thing has cooled. Care like that exhausts you and starts to squeeze the thing you're caring for. The way back is tending done well: growth happening without forcing, holding space without clutching, letting what's planted do its own growing.
cells.sheetLine: Loosening your grip isn't quitting. It's tending well.
cells.verb: Feeling a thing through until it's whole, and knowing it's whole.

cells.tense: Something you made is finished and you haven't stood in that finish; you're still facing the door you already walked through.
cells.ask: Sit with the result of something you made for ten minutes, no plan and no verdict, then write one sentence about what you notice. It gives back a finish you didn't stop for.
cells.core:
On an ordinary good week you can say the true thing about what you made — that it's good, or it isn't, or it's finished — without dressing it up, and then you move on. You know what you think before you're asked, and that's enough for the next step.

Right now you're not landing on any verdict, and lately nothing gets marked finished even when it is. Pushing yourself back into the making won't work, because what's starved isn't the making: it's the time you give to what's already sitting there to be looked at. Nothing you build will satisfy you until looking gets room again. The way back is letting what you made tell you what it is before you decide, and being easy with not knowing yet.
cells.sheetLine: Before the next push, give what you made its ten minutes.
cells.verb: Feeling a thing through until it's whole, and knowing it's whole.

cells.tense: You're calling what you've made unfinished, and the satisfaction of it is running as though it belonged to the next thing.
cells.ask: Take something finished and give it one honest sentence in your own voice, then leave it alone. The sentence is the act. It hands the whole feeling back to you.
cells.core:
On an ordinary good week you can tell a real next step from a reason to keep polishing, and you take the one that grows the work. You can sit with what you've made long enough to hear what it actually needs, and that time alone feeds the work instead of feeding worry.

What looks like getting ready is the same want on a longer delay: it isn't gone, it's aimed at the future. Going over what's done is the shape your satisfaction has taken, and the practice is real, but it isn't feeding the making. The way back is picking what matters, dropping the rest, and letting the picking be yours.

cells.verb: Feeling a thing through until it's whole, and knowing it's whole.
cells.place: The place where a thing is finished and let go from, which is also where the next one starts.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim I have to watch is the story-lure: I do not know whether anyone in their life is watching what they finish, so the cells may locate the watching only as a possibility, never as fact. The reader might say completion has never been the problem, or that feeling good about something already made does not apply here, so the asks stay useful even if my read is off: the test should teach them something about their own finish line whether or not the diagnosis lands. The sentence that serves me more than them is any poetic line about fits or gratitude — I cut every one, and the closing lines do the work in plain speech.
